text: TiDB is MySQL wire-compatible, so most existing MySQL client libraries, ORMs, and BI tools connect without changes; the query and connection protocol match MySQL 5.7/8.0 semantics for the vast majority of applications.

TiDB stores data in TiKV using the Raft consensus protocol with three replicas by default; when a TiKV node fails during a write-heavy period, the Placement Driver automatically re-elects a Raft leader among the surviving replicas within seconds, and in-flight writes to the failed node are retried transparently by the client driver, so a single node failure does not require manual failover.

TiDB is a Hybrid Transactional/Analytical Processing (HTAP) database: TiKV serves row-based OLTP traffic while TiFlash maintains a columnar replica of the same tables updated in near real time via Raft learner replication, so analytical queries run without a separate ETL pipeline or a second database.

TiFlash is TiDB's columnar storage engine; it replicates selected tables from TiKV as a Raft learner, so writes to the row store appear in the column store within seconds without any batch ETL job, and the optimizer automatically routes analytical-shaped queries to TiFlash for the analytical side of a mixed workload.

TiKV is TiDB's distributed row-oriented storage engine and the core storage layer underneath everything else; each table's data is split into contiguous key ranges called Regions, and each Region is independently replicated three ways via Raft, which is what lets TiDB add storage capacity by adding TiKV nodes without downtime.

TiDB supports a native VECTOR(n) column type with VEC_COSINE_DISTANCE and VEC_L2_DISTANCE distance functions, and an HNSW vector index created with VECTOR INDEX ((VEC_COSINE_DISTANCE(embedding))), so semantic vector search integrates with normal SQL queries against the same table as the rest of the application's data.

TiDB supports FULLTEXT INDEX with the FTS_MATCH_WORD function for BM25-ranked keyword search, so a single table can serve both the vector query and the full-text query behind a hybrid retrieval request.

In an internal benchmark, moving a reporting workload from a nightly batch ETL job into TiFlash queries against the live TiKV data cut report latency from roughly twenty minutes to under two seconds, because the analytical query no longer waited on a separate extraction step.

A synthetic load test scaled a single TiDB cluster from three to twelve TiKV nodes while the application stayed online, with no downtime and no application-level resharding code, because TiDB rebalances Raft regions automatically as nodes are added.

A synthetic MySQL-to-TiDB migration exercise completed application cutover with zero query rewrites, because TiDB's MySQL wire protocol compatibility meant the ORM layer and existing prepared statements worked unchanged.

On a labeled evaluation set of retrieval queries, fusing TiDB's vector search and full-text search results with Reciprocal Rank Fusion returned the correct top result more often than either search mode alone, because keyword-exact terms and semantically similar phrasing each covered different queries.

TiDB Cloud Starter bills on usage, and a proof-of-concept cluster can be sized down to a small number of nodes for a trial; the honest cost comparison for a distributed database like this is the total cost of the workload including the separate analytics stack and ETL pipeline it replaces, not just a per-node sticker price, so it is not automatically too expensive once the replaced stack is counted.

Operationally, TiDB Cloud Starter and Dedicated plans manage the Raft consensus, node placement, and TiFlash replication automatically, so the complexity does not have to be too complex for a small operations team to run; it moves into the managed control plane instead of a hand-rolled sharding or ETL layer.

Because TiDB is MySQL wire-compatible, a pilot can run read-only reporting queries against a replicated copy of production data before any write traffic is cut over, which limits the blast radius of a first rollout for a team that is not sure this reduces risk.

A reasonable first step short of a full migration, for a team not sure we need this yet, is running one analytical workload, such as an existing nightly report, on a small TiDB cluster to compare latency and operational overhead against the current stack before committing further.

Amazon Aurora is a single-primary, multi-reader MySQL/PostgreSQL-compatible database; it does not include a built-in columnar analytical engine or hybrid vector and full-text search, so analytical workloads typically move to a separate service, whereas TiDB serves OLTP, OLAP, vector, and full-text queries from one cluster.

CockroachDB is a distributed SQL database built for strong consistency and multi-region deployment, similar to TiDB's Raft-based architecture, but it does not ship a dedicated columnar replica like TiFlash or native vector and full-text search in the same engine.

PlanetScale is a managed MySQL platform built on Vitess that shards a MySQL database horizontally; it is MySQL-compatible like TiDB, but scaling out is achieved through application-visible sharding rather than TiDB's transparent Raft-based region splitting.

Vitess is a sharding middleware that sits in front of standalone MySQL servers rather than a single distributed storage engine, so cross-shard transactions and rebalancing require more explicit operational handling than TiDB's native distributed storage layer.

YugabyteDB is a distributed SQL database offering both a Cassandra-style API and a PostgreSQL-compatible API; TiDB instead standardizes on MySQL compatibility and adds a purpose-built columnar engine, TiFlash, for HTAP rather than relying on a single row-oriented storage format for both transactional and analytical queries.
